title: Honest business
hookLine: just prices, true words, fair deals
tomorrow: why is rest a commandment and not a reward?

cards: An online listing asks one small question: condition? A tear inside the lining won't show in any photo. Markets have always had moments like that.

In the old markets, a seller weighed goods on a hand scale against stones carried in a bag. And the law of Moses reaches right into that bag. You shall not keep two weights there, Deuteronomy says, a greater and a less.
Some readers explain it simply: one stone for buying, one for selling, and the buyer never sees both. The law cared anyway.

teach.b: So a Bible law cares about a merchant's bag because cheating there is quiet. Nobody sees the second stone.

teach.h: A JUST WEIGHT IS HIS WILL.
teach.b: Proverbs puts it in the strongest words, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord: and a just weight is his will." God's will, located in a scale.
That's honest business in its first form: a just price, the same weight on both sides of the counter. Its second form is the true word.
Jesus says, "let your speech be yea, yea: no, no." A yes that means yes, a condition that means the condition. Its third form is the fair deal, and Luke gives it a face.
Zacchaeus, a tax collector, climbs down from a tree to host Jesus, and stands up at his own table to say, "if I have wronged any man of any thing, I restore him fourfold."
He says it standing, out loud, in front of a crowd that had grumbled about him. He doesn't promise to cheat less from now on. He goes back for what was taken.

The Catechism keeps the list current: it names business fraud, unjust wages, and raising prices by taking advantage of someone's ignorance or hardship. The scale has changed shape. The stones are still in somebody's bag.

how: Catholic social teaching applies the seventh commandment to business: just prices, honest contracts, fair wages, and restitution for what was wrongly taken.

o: a company the Church owns and runs
fair prices, true words and fair deals
work done only for a charity

s: the Bible keeps its concern with honesty for the temple, not the market
Deuteronomy and Proverbs go straight to the merchant's bag and scale.
the Catechism names raising prices on someone's hardship as wrong
CCC 2409 lists it beside business fraud and unjust wages.
Zacchaeus promised to pay back exactly what he took
he says he restores fourfold to anyone he wronged.

games.q: at your summer job, the manager says to keep yesterday's muffins in the case at full price, labeled 'fresh baked.' what fits honest dealing?
o: ask to label them day-old, or price them lower.
sell them as labeled; the sign is the manager's call.
throw them all out so nobody gets cheated.
games.why: a true label is the just weight. honest business doesn't mean wasting good food; it means saying what the thing is and pricing it fairly.

practice: Pick up two small things, one in each hand: a phone and a cup, a book and a pen. Close your fingers around each and feel which is heavier, until the hands agree.
Then bring to mind one deal this week, a sale, a trade, a promise at work, and feel where it needs a true weight.

wordCard.voice: Honest business. Just prices, true words and fair deals, one weight for the buyer and the seller alike, whether the bag holds stones or a listing holds photos.

orig.note: Latin, Proverbs 11:1 in the Vulgate: a just weight, which the verse calls God's will.

carryVoice: Your line: honest dealing. One stone in the bag, for buying and for selling. Until tomorrow.
